title: Understanding Cross-layer Contributions to Mixture-of-Experts Routing in LLMs
claim: A component's routing score decomposes recursively into contributions from all earlier components, and further into fine-grained units.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right layer blocks, red arrows converging on target expert
description: A single wide diagram of a transformer stack drawn as colored rounded boxes: a green Token Embedding, then pairs of yellow Attention and blue MoE layers grouped in black outlines (Layer 1, ellipsis, Layer l-1, Layer l). On the right is a teal circle labeled 'Expert in MoE Layer l'. Thick red arrows arc over the top from the token embedding and every earlier attention and MoE block into this expert circle. A red-and-colored caption at top left (1) explains that the expert's assignment score splits into sub-scores from tokens, attention and FFN. Below, dashed orange lines link attention layers to small orange squares labeled Attention Heads, and dashed cyan lines link MoE layers to small teal circles labeled Experts. A caption at bottom right (2) says scores can be decomposed further into heads or experts. The red arrows draw the eye first.
caption: Overview of the decomposition of experts assignment scores.
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has been a prevalent method for scaling up large language models at a reduced computational cost. Despite its effectiveness, the routing mechanism of MoE still lacks a clear understanding from the perspective of cross-layer mechanistic interpretability. We propose a light-weight methodology at which we can break down the routing decision for MoE to the contribution of model components, in a recursive fashion. We use our methodology to dissect the routing mechanism by decomposing the input of routers into model components. We study how different model components contribute to the routing in different widely used open models. Our findings on four different LLMs reveal patterns such as: a) MoE layer outputs usually contribute more than attention layer outputs to the routing decisions of subsequent layers, b) MoE entanglement at which MoE firing up in layers consistently correlate with firing up of MoE in subsequent layers, and c) some components can persistently influence the routing in many following layers. Our study also includes findings on how different models have different patterns when it comes to long-range and short-range inhibiting/promoting effects that components can have over MoE in subsequent layers. Our results indicate the importance of quantifying the impact of components across different layers on MoE to understand the routing mechanism.
